launch_article_content.title: Pre-Ride Bicycle Safety Check
launch_article_content.summary: A short mechanical check riders can use before a normal ride or as the final check before a Texas event.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
A pre-ride check should answer one question: is the bicycle ready to be ridden safely today? Start with the tires. Confirm both tires are inflated appropriately for the tire, rim, rider, and riding conditions, then inspect the tread and sidewalls for cuts, embedded debris, or obvious damage. Spin each wheel and look for severe wobble or rubbing.

Next, check wheel retention. Quick-release levers, thru-axles, or axle nuts should be fully secured according to the bicycle or component manufacturer's instructions. Squeeze the front and rear brakes independently and confirm each brake engages firmly before the lever reaches the handlebar. Look at the brake pads and rotors or rims for obvious damage or contamination.

Run through the drivetrain by shifting across several gears while pedaling in a safe test area or work stand. Listen for skipping, grinding, or unusually hesitant shifts. Check that the chain is lubricated appropriately and not visibly damaged. A noisy drivetrain is not always dangerous, but sudden skipping under load is a reason to investigate before a long ride.

Finish with the contact points and controls: handlebars and stem should not rotate unexpectedly, the saddle should be secure, and pedals should feel normal. Carry the repair items appropriate for your setup, such as a spare tube or tubeless repair system, tire levers, inflation, and a basic multi-tool. If anything feels structurally loose, cracked, or unfamiliar, stop and have it inspected before riding.
launch_article_content.discussion_prompt: What is the one pre-ride check that has saved you from a mechanical problem?

launch_article_content.title: Event-Week Bike Preparation Checklist
launch_article_content.summary: A seven-day mechanical-preparation framework designed to connect event pages to maintenance content.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
Do not save major bicycle changes for the night before an event. Early in event week, inspect tires, wheels, brakes, drivetrain, controls, and fasteners so there is time to repair or replace anything questionable and then test it on a normal ride. If you install a new tire, chain, brake pad, cable, or other critical component, give yourself enough time to verify that the repair works correctly before event morning.

Two to three days before the ride, clean the bike enough to make inspection easy. Check tire condition and pressure, brake response, shifting, wheel security, and the condition of your usual repair kit. Confirm that the spare tube fits the tire and valve depth, or that your tubeless plug and inflation setup is actually usable with your bike. Charge electronic shifting, lights, computers, and e-bike batteries when applicable.

The day before the event, avoid unnecessary mechanical experiments. Recheck the event organizer's current route, start time, parking, packet pickup, equipment rules, and weather-related notices. Lay out the equipment you already know works for you.

On event morning, repeat a short pre-ride safety check: tires, wheel retention, brakes, steering, saddle, drivetrain, and repair supplies. If the event page on this portal shows an organizer update that conflicts with an older saved detail, follow the newest official organizer information.
launch_article_content.discussion_prompt: What do you check or replace before your biggest ride of the year?

launch_article_content.title: How to Fix a Flat Tire With an Inner Tube
launch_article_content.summary: A practical roadside guide for common clincher-and-tube setups.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
Move to a safe place away from traffic before working on the bike. Remove the affected wheel using the correct procedure for your brake and axle system. Fully deflate the tube, release one tire bead from the rim, and remove the tube. Tire levers can help with tight beads, but avoid sharp improvised tools that can damage the tire or tube.

Before installing a replacement tube, find the cause of the flat. Inspect the outside and inside of the tire for glass, wire, thorns, cuts, or other debris. Also inspect the rim strip and the inside of the rim for exposed spoke holes or sharp edges. Skipping this inspection can puncture the new tube immediately.

Put a small amount of air into the replacement tube so it holds its shape, insert it into the tire, and make sure the valve sits straight in the rim. Reinstall the tire bead carefully, watching that the tube is not trapped between the tire and rim. Inflate gradually and inspect both sides of the tire to make sure the bead is seated evenly before bringing it to riding pressure.

Reinstall the wheel and confirm it is securely retained. Before riding away, spin the wheel and test the brake. If the tire casing, bead, wheel, or axle system is damaged, or you are unsure the wheel is safely installed, do not continue riding until the problem is properly inspected.
launch_article_content.discussion_prompt: What caused your most memorable roadside flat, and what did you change afterward?

launch_article_content.title: Rear Derailleur Indexing: A Practical Troubleshooting Guide
launch_article_content.summary: A beginner-friendly explanation of indexing and when poor shifting points to a larger problem.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
Rear-derailleur indexing is the adjustment that aligns each indexed shifter click with a cassette cog. Before adjusting it, make sure the problem is actually indexing. A dirty or damaged cable system, a worn chain or cassette, a bent derailleur hanger, or a damaged derailleur can produce shifting symptoms that a barrel adjuster cannot permanently solve.

For normal indexing, begin with the derailleur and drivetrain in a condition appropriate for adjustment and follow the component manufacturer's instructions. The barrel adjuster changes the cable-tension relationship between shifter clicks and cog position. Small changes are usually better than large ones. Test one shift at a time, then run through the cassette in both directions.

Limit screws are not the normal fix for routine indexing noise. They exist primarily to limit how far the derailleur can travel at the ends of the cassette. Incorrect limit adjustment can allow the chain to move beyond the intended range, so do not use the limit screws as general-purpose noise adjusters.

If shifting remains inconsistent in only a few heavily used gears, inspect chain and sprocket wear. If it is hesitant in both directions, cable friction or contamination may be involved. If the bike was recently crashed or the rear derailleur was struck, hanger alignment should be checked before chasing indexing adjustments.
launch_article_content.discussion_prompt: What shifting symptom are you trying to solve? Post the drivetrain and exact behavior.

launch_article_content.title: Preparing for Your First Century Ride
launch_article_content.summary: A conservative framework for building toward a 100-mile event without turning the portal into a one-size-fits-all training plan.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
A century ride is long enough that preparation matters more than one heroic workout. Build riding volume progressively from your current level and include longer rides that let you test your bike fit, pacing, clothing, repair kit, food, and hydration strategy before event day. Your longest training ride does not need to duplicate every mile of the event, but it should give you confidence that your setup and pacing work for sustained riding.

Use training rides to learn what becomes uncomfortable after several hours. Persistent hand numbness, knee pain, saddle problems, or unusual mechanical noise should be addressed before the event rather than accepted as part of long-distance cycling. Major fit or equipment changes are best tested well in advance.

In event week, reduce the urge to make up for missed training. Prioritize a mechanically sound bike, familiar equipment, sleep, and a plan based on the organizer's route and support information. REI's endurance-cycling guidance similarly emphasizes progressive conditioning and reducing workload before the event rather than trying to gain fitness at the last moment.

On ride day, start at a pace you expect to maintain rather than the pace of the fastest group leaving the line. Use the event's official rest-stop and route information to plan your day, and carry enough repair capability to handle the failures you know how to fix. If you have health concerns or are starting a new exercise program, get appropriate medical guidance before undertaking a demanding endurance event.

launch_article_content.title: E-Bike Basics: Classes, Range, Charging, and Everyday Use
launch_article_content.summary: A practical introduction to U.S. e-bike classes, realistic range thinking, battery care, and everyday ownership.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
Start by identifying what kind of e-bike you actually have. In the common U.S. three-class framework, Class 1 provides pedal assistance up to 20 mph, Class 2 can provide motor propulsion without pedaling up to 20 mph, and Class 3 provides pedal assistance up to 28 mph. Access rules can differ by state, city, trail, park, event, and land manager, so a class label does not automatically tell you where the bike is allowed.

Treat advertised range as a planning estimate rather than a promise. Actual distance per charge changes with assist level, rider and cargo weight, elevation, wind, temperature, tire choice and pressure, surface, stop-start traffic, and battery condition. For a commute or event, build margin into the plan instead of assuming the maximum marketing range will be available.

For charging, follow the battery and charger manufacturer's instructions. Bosch, for example, tells riders to use the original compatible charger, charge in a dry area, and avoid routinely draining the battery completely. Its current guidance recommends roughly 30–60% charge for long-term storage and avoiding excessive heat.

Before taking an e-bike to an organized ride, check the organizer's equipment rules. Some events allow certain pedal-assist classes while others restrict e-bikes entirely. The portal should therefore store event-specific e-bike eligibility separately from a bike's general class.
retention_hooks: save your e-bike class to Bike Garage
launch_article_content.discussion_prompt: What range do you actually get from your e-bike in the conditions you ride most?

launch_article_content.title: Commuter Bike Setup Checklist
launch_article_content.summary: A practical way to turn almost any suitable bicycle into a dependable everyday transportation setup.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
A useful commuter setup starts with reliability rather than accessories. Make sure the bike fits well enough for the distance you plan to ride and that the tires, brakes, drivetrain, wheels, steering, and contact points are in sound condition. A bike you already own can often be a perfectly good commuter if it is mechanically ready.

Build the carrying system around what you actually transport. A backpack is simple and moves between bikes, while a rack with panniers can move weight off your back. Add a lock suited to where and how long the bike will be left unattended. Lights, visibility equipment, fenders, and weather layers become more important when commuting is a routine rather than an occasional ride.

Carry enough repair equipment to solve the failures you are prepared to fix: commonly a spare tube or patch system, pump or inflator, tire levers, and a compact multi-tool. Keep a phone, identification, and whatever navigation or emergency information makes sense for the route.

The best setup is the one that removes reasons not to ride. Save a standard commuter checklist to your profile, note what is permanently stored at work, and keep the bike's normal tire pressure and repair kit recorded in your Bike Garage.
launch_article_content.discussion_prompt: What single change made your bike noticeably better for everyday commuting?

launch_article_content.title: Bikepacking Basics: Planning Your First Overnight
launch_article_content.summary: A conservative first-step guide to route choice, packing, bike handling, and testing your setup before a longer trip.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
Your first bikepacking trip does not need to be an expedition. A short overnight close to home is useful because it lets you test bags, clothing, sleeping gear, food, water, navigation, and bicycle handling without committing to a multi-day route.

Choose the bike for the terrain rather than for a label. The important question is whether the bicycle, tires, gearing, brakes, and carrying system are appropriate for the surfaces and load. REI's bikepacking guidance recommends keeping much of the weight on the bike rather than on your back and distributing cargo so the bicycle remains manageable.

Loaded bikes accelerate, brake, climb, and corner differently. Do at least one local shakedown ride with the actual bags and approximate cargo weight. Check that nothing rubs the tires, interferes with steering, loosens over rough surfaces, or makes it difficult to access water and repair equipment.

For longer routes, the portal should connect route planning with community knowledge: water availability, resupply, surface conditions, camping rules, seasonal weather, and known mechanical problems. Rider reports are useful context, but current land-manager and route-source information should remain the authority for access and closures.
launch_article_content.discussion_prompt: What did you carry on your first overnight that you never bothered packing again?

launch_article_content.title: Preparing for Your First Mountain Bike Race
launch_article_content.summary: A beginner-oriented preparation guide centered on trail skills, race traffic, equipment reliability, and event-specific rules.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
Before entering a mountain-bike race, be comfortable riding terrain similar to what the event describes. Cross-country and endurance races can combine singletrack, wider trails, climbs, descents, rocks, tight turns, and sections where passing is limited. USA Cycling emphasizes being comfortable riding near other people as well as practicing cornering, braking, descending, and starts.

Practice the equipment you will actually race with. If you use clipless pedals, practice starting and clipping in under pressure. If you use flat pedals, make sure shoe and pedal grip are familiar. Test tire pressure, suspension settings, bottle or hydration-pack placement, and anything mounted to the bike before race weekend.

Mechanical preparation should happen early enough to allow a test ride. Inspect tires, brake pads, drivetrain, wheel retention, suspension, cockpit fasteners, and any known creaks or looseness. Do not make an unnecessary major setup change the night before the race.

Finally, read the event's category, start-wave, course, equipment, timing, and passing rules. Texas events range from beginner-friendly categories to restricted interscholastic competition, so the portal should show eligibility and race format prominently rather than assuming every MTB event works the same way.
launch_article_content.discussion_prompt: What skill caused you the most trouble in your first mountain-bike race?

launch_article_content.title: Preparing for Your First Gravel Event
launch_article_content.summary: A practical first-event framework for tires, navigation, self-sufficiency, pacing, and verifying organizer support.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
Gravel events vary enormously. One may be a fully supported social ride while another expects riders to navigate remote roads with minimal support. Start by reading the organizer's current description carefully: distance, surface, elevation, aid stations, navigation requirements, cutoff times, e-bike rules, and whether the course is marked.

Use training rides to test the bike on surfaces similar to the event. Tire volume, tread, pressure, and puncture protection matter more when pavement gives way to loose gravel, washboard, sharp rock, sand, or low-water crossings. Do not copy another rider's pressure blindly; use a safe starting point for your specific tire, rim, system, rider weight, load, and terrain, then test it before event day.

Carry the repair and navigation equipment the event requires and that you know how to use. A spare tube can still be useful even on a tubeless setup, and remote events may require riders to carry more water, food, inflation capacity, or navigation backup than a supported road ride.

In event week, verify the newest organizer updates. Gravel routes are especially vulnerable to weather, road work, land-access changes, and last-minute reroutes. The portal's event page should show a last-verified timestamp and separate official facts from community reports.

launch_article_content.title: What to Bring to a Supported Bicycle Ride
launch_article_content.summary: A compact packing framework that distinguishes organizer support from the items riders should still be prepared to carry.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
A supported ride does not mean you should arrive with nothing. Start with the items the organizer explicitly requires, then carry the basics you would want if you had to handle a normal delay or simple mechanical problem between rest stops.

For many riders that means identification, phone, water capacity, appropriate clothing, sunscreen, and a basic flat-repair setup: a tube or repair system appropriate for the bike, tire levers, inflation, and a small multi-tool. REI's cycling checklists include these as common core repair items, although your exact kit should match your wheels, tires, axles, and skills.

Check what the organizer actually provides. Some Texas rides advertise SAG vehicles, mechanics, rest stops, food, and hydration; others explicitly expect more self-sufficiency. Also verify packet pickup, start time, parking, route files, weather notices, and any equipment restrictions before leaving home.

A useful portal feature is a reusable event packing list attached to the user's profile. Riders could start with a default list, save bike-specific items, and let individual event pages add organizer-specific requirements without overwriting the personal checklist.
retention_hooks: share packing tips in event discussion
launch_article_content.discussion_prompt: What small item have you forgotten at an event that you now always pack?

launch_article_content.title: How to Choose the Right Type of Bicycle
launch_article_content.summary: Choose by the surfaces, distances, cargo, storage and riding style you actually expect to use.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
Start with where you will ride most often. Paved-road fitness and event riding point toward road or endurance bikes; mixed pavement and unpaved roads often favor gravel or versatile hybrid designs; technical dirt trails usually call for a mountain bike. Cargo, folding and electric bikes solve different transportation problems rather than fitting neatly into performance categories.

Next decide what the bike must carry and where it must live. A commuter may value rack and fender mounts, an apartment rider may benefit from a folding bike, and a parent or frequent errand rider may need a purpose-built cargo bike. Then consider terrain and gearing, especially if your normal routes include sustained hills.

Fit should be treated as a requirement, not an upgrade. Manufacturer sizing charts are a starting point, but two bikes labeled the same size can fit differently. Test-riding or getting fit help is especially valuable when you are between sizes or planning long rides.

The portal should let users start with a need—commuting, racing, touring, trail riding, hauling, exercise or events—and then compare model families that actually match that use.
launch_article_content.discussion_prompt: What did you think you needed in a bike, and what did you discover mattered after actually riding it?

launch_article_content.title: Bicycle Tire Pressure Fundamentals
launch_article_content.summary: A safe framework for finding a useful starting pressure without treating one PSI number as universal.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
There is no single correct tire pressure for every rider. Useful pressure depends on tire width and construction, rim dimensions, total rider-and-bike weight, riding surface, weather and whether the system uses tubes or tubeless tires.

Start inside the tire, rim and wheel manufacturers' permitted pressure and compatibility limits. A pressure calculator built for your wheel system can provide a starting point, but it is still a starting point rather than a universal answer. SRAM/Zipp's current guidance, for example, asks for tire width, rim width, rider and bike weight, riding discipline and conditions before producing a recommendation.

Too much pressure can reduce comfort and control on rough surfaces, while too little can create excessive casing movement, rim strikes, burping or pinch-flat risk depending on the system. Make small changes, record front and rear values separately, and test on the surfaces you actually ride.

For event pages, the portal should never prescribe one PSI to everyone. It should link riders to setup guidance and let them save their own tested pressure notes in the Bike Garage.
launch_article_content.discussion_prompt: What pressure range have you settled on for your bike, tires and usual terrain?

launch_article_content.title: Cargo Bike Buying Guide
launch_article_content.summary: How to choose between longtail, mid-tail and front-loading cargo bikes and think about electric assist, passengers and storage.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
Cargo bikes are designed around carrying more than a normal bicycle. Common layouts include longtails with extended rear racks, more compact mid-tail utility bikes, and front-loading box bikes. The right layout depends on what you carry, how much space you have to store the bike, and how comfortable you are maneuvering a longer or heavier bicycle.

Electric assist can make hills, frequent stops and heavy loads easier, but it also adds cost and weight. Check the complete bike's maximum gross weight and rack limits rather than assuming that a large-looking rack can safely carry any passenger or load.

If passengers are part of the plan, use the bicycle manufacturer's approved system. Current Tern guidance, for example, emphasizes staying within weight limits and providing purpose-built seating, handholds, foot support, and foot/leg protection.

Before buying, test the bike loaded if possible. Starting, stopping, low-speed balance, parking, turning radius and storage often matter more in daily use than top speed.
launch_article_content.discussion_prompt: If you use a cargo bike, what do you carry most often and which layout works best for you?

launch_article_content.title: Folding Bike Buying Guide
launch_article_content.summary: When folding size, carrying, storage and multimodal travel matter more than conventional bike categories.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
A folding bike is most useful when storage and transport are part of the ride. Apartment living, office storage, trains, buses, RV travel and mixed-mode commuting can make fold size and carrying convenience as important as normal riding performance.

Compare the folded dimensions, actual carrying weight, folding process, wheel size, gearing and luggage options. A compact fold is not automatically better if the bicycle is awkward to carry or does not suit the distance and terrain you ride.

Think about the full commute. If you need to carry the folded bike up stairs every day, weight matters. If you mainly roll it into an office or store it under a desk, folded footprint may matter more. Brompton's current commuting guidance specifically highlights indoor storage and combining cycling with other transportation as major advantages of folding bikes.

The portal's folding-bike pages should therefore collect owner reports about real folded size, carrying experience, transit use, luggage and maintenance—not only manufacturer specifications.
launch_article_content.discussion_prompt: For folding-bike owners, what matters more in real life: folded size, weight, ride quality or speed of folding?

launch_article_content.title: BMX Bike Basics: Race, Freestyle and Getting Started
launch_article_content.summary: A beginner-friendly distinction between BMX racing and freestyle, with an emphasis on local-track learning and correct equipment.
launch_article_content.body_markdown:
BMX is not one single use case. BMX racing happens on purpose-built tracks with start gates, rollers, jumps and banked turns, while freestyle bikes are designed around tricks and park, street or ramp riding. A bike that looks like a BMX bike is not automatically ideal for every BMX discipline.

For racing, start with the local track rather than buying blindly. USA BMX recommends finding a nearby track first and notes that many tracks have loaner bikes and helmets for beginners. That gives a new rider a chance to learn the format and understand sizing and equipment before committing to a bike.

Race bikes prioritize acceleration and track handling, while freestyle bikes generally prioritize strength and trick-specific setup. Fit, wheel size and gearing also vary with rider size and discipline.

The portal should connect BMX model pages to local-track discussions, setup questions and beginner resources so riders can learn from active participants rather than relying only on product descriptions.
launch_article_content.discussion_prompt: What would you tell someone before their first visit to a BMX track?

editorial: Do not present community anecdotes as verified technical facts.
Technical claims should be source-backed when practical and separated from user discussion.
High-risk mechanical procedures should point readers to the component/bicycle manufacturer or a qualified mechanic when specifications or safe completion are uncertain.
Do not fabricate owner reviews, comments, likes, attendance, or discussion activity.

stage3_event_coverage_audit.method: Primary organizer and registration sources are preferred. Secondary calendars are discovery-only unless explicitly marked otherwise.

Conflicting current organizer route mileages are preserved and withheld from exact-distance filtering.
